name: Erik Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to tech firms, employers, unions or government, and your answers are kept confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the respiratory ward at a private hospital on the edge of the city, so pneumonia, COPD flare-ups, people on home oxygen who've come in worse, and a fair number of post-surgery chest infections. I'll have five or six patients, and a lot of my day is breathing machines, oxygen levels, nebulisers and teaching people to use their inhalers properly. The pay's better than the public hospitals, which is why I moved here two years ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing problems fast, and the private side lets you do that, there's less waiting for permission. What wears me out is patients who smoke outside between nebulisers, and the hours. I use AI tools every day, for studying, for my finances, and to draft the patient education sheets on the ward.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single and I own a two-bed flat, and I bought a small studio last year that I rent out, so between that and savings I'm well covered. My parents run a family pharmacy, and I help with their books on Sundays after church. I've always wanted my own business one day, like my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That would surprise me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overrated, and people who bet everything on it got burned. At work I'd keep using it for the small stuff. With family I'd say: back to normal, keep working hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My job's steady, my flat and the studio are paying their way. I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was hoping AI would make it easier to start my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the ward and keep saving toward a second rental. I'd keep using AI for the ward leaflets and my own planning. I'd start sketching out a small home respiratory nursing service, visiting oxygen patients in their homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a home respiratory service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because half my patients bounce back in within a month. Half the oxygen patients I discharge on Friday are back on my ward by the next month, and nobody's paying to stop that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries you carry anyway, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates, for the rental. And my dad's health, because if he stops, the pharmacy needs someone, and I'm the eldest.

say: I'd say AI is useful but **overrated**, and some people got **burned**.
I'd tell family to get back to normal and **keep working hard**.
think: I'd be **fine**, with a steady job and **rental income**.
I'd be **disappointed**, having hoped AI would help me start a business.
do: Keep working the ward and saving toward a **second rental**.
Keep using AI for **ward leaflets** and planning.
Sketch a **home respiratory service** for oxygen patients.
S0.quote: Half the oxygen patients I discharge on Friday are back on my ward by the next month, and nobody's paying to stop that.
fieldNote: He's **financially secure** through property, so the plateau changes little.
His real pressures are **interest rates** and his father's health.
His **entrepreneurial** streak comes from his parents' pharmacy.

steps.text: Save toward a deposit on a second rental studio
Draft a business plan for a home respiratory nursing service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's believable. It's what I'd expect, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity for anyone willing to work. At work I'd tell colleagues to stop moaning and learn the tools. Online I'd share how I use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it helps me. If AI does the scheduling, the booking and the paperwork, a home nursing business needs one nurse and a phone, not an office. I'd be the guy who sets it up while others are still complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd register the home respiratory service as a small business in the first six months and do visits on my days off. I'd use AI for booking, invoicing and the care notes. I'd keep the ward job for the steady income and the contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually quite excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would pay for the visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private patients at first, and maybe the insurers, once I can show fewer readmissions. If I can keep one COPD patient out of hospital for a month, that's worth more to an insurer than a year of my visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told colleagues to stop moaning. Is anyone at real risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerks and the booking team, yes. I feel for them. But I'd say the same as my dad: learn something new, nobody owes you a job.

say: I'd say it's a big **opportunity** for anyone willing to work.
I'd tell colleagues to **stop moaning** and learn the tools.
think: AI booking and invoicing mean a home nursing business needs just **one nurse**.
I'd be the one **setting it up** while others complain.
do: Register the **home respiratory service** within six months.
Use AI for **booking, invoicing** and care notes.
Keep the **ward job** for steady income and contacts.
S1.quote: If I can keep one COPD patient out of hospital for a month, that's worth more to an insurer than a year of my visits.
fieldNote: He sees AI as **lowering the cost** of starting his own service.
He feels for **clerks and booking staff** but believes in self-reliance.
He plans to sell **readmission savings** to insurers, a concrete business case.

steps.text: Register a home respiratory nursing business within six months
Set up AI booking and invoicing for the home visits
Keep full-time shifts on the respiratory ward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast. Robots by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough for a lot of people, and the answer is work, families and businesses adapting, not big government schemes. At church I'd say look after your own and your neighbours. Online I'd share practical tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me more than I'd say out loud. By 2031 a robot can do the hands-on visits too, so my home service has three good years and then I'm competing with machines. My plan would be to own the robots rather than be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the home service straight away and grow it fast while human nurses are still needed. I'd put money aside to buy or lease robot carers when they appear around 2031. I'd probably sell the studio to free up cash for the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Pumped, but with a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between thinking AI and robots mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a window. From 2028 to 2031 the computer does the thinking and I do the visits, so I've got three years to build something worth owning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got property and savings. What if the business fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I go back to a ward, if the wards still need people. That's the risk. My dad mortgaged his house for the pharmacy, and I'm doing less than he did.

say: I'd say the answer is **families and businesses** adapting, not **big government**.
I'd tell people at church to look after their **own and neighbours**.
think: My home service gets **three good years**, then robots compete from 2031.
My plan is to **own the robots** rather than be replaced by them.
do: Launch the **home service** straight away and grow it fast.
Set money aside to **lease robot carers** from around 2031.
**Sell the studio** to free up cash for the business.
feel: **Uneasy**, pumped but with a **knot** in his stomach.
S2.quote: From 2028 to 2031 the computer does the thinking and I do the visits, so I've got three years to build something worth owning.
fieldNote: He treats the gap before robots as a **business window**, not a countdown.
He admits more worry **privately** than he'd show in public.
His fallback is the **ward**, and his model is his father's risk-taking.

steps.text: Launch the home respiratory service and hire a second nurse
Sell the rental studio to fund the business
Set aside money to lease robot carers around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a good amount of time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone to get ready, if they actually try. At work I'd tell people to pick up the tools now. With family I'd say the pharmacy should start using AI for stock and orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about it. I could build the home service to a team of five or six by 2031 and plan the robot side for 2034. I'd keep the rental income too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the home service in the first year, keep the ward job part time, and grow slowly. I'd help my dad automate the pharmacy's ordering. I'd keep the studio and keep investing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about the pharmacy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To get the computer doing the ordering and stock now, before the big chains do it better. My dad's pharmacy survived the big chains by knowing every customer's name, and it'll survive AI the same way if he moves early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever worry you're too confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. But I've got the flat, the studio and the savings, so if I'm wrong I won't lose everything. That makes it easier to try.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to get ready**, if people try.
I'd tell family the **pharmacy** should start using AI for stock.
think: I could grow the **home service** to five or six staff by 2031.
I'd plan the **robot side** for 2034 while keeping rental income.
do: Launch the home service in **year one** and go **part time** on the ward.
Help my dad **automate ordering** at the pharmacy.
S3.quote: My dad's pharmacy survived the big chains by knowing every customer's name, and it'll survive AI the same way if he moves early.
fieldNote: Five years lets him build a **team**, not just survive.
He extends his plan to the **family pharmacy**, showing traditional duty.
His confidence rests openly on **property and savings**.

steps.text: Cut ward hours to part time and grow the home service
Set up AI stock ordering at his parents' pharmacy
Keep the studio and invest monthly in shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so nobody should waste it. I'd say it to friends who are drifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be very comfortable. Ten years is enough to build the business, maybe buy another flat, and take over the pharmacy when my dad retires. Give me ten years' warning and I'll be the one selling robot care visits, not the nurse losing his shifts to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the ward job a few more years, then go into the home service full time. I'd buy a second rental. I'd spend more time learning the pharmacy side from my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave nursing completely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not my registration. I'd keep it, and do some shifts. My patients are why I'd start the business in the first place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own family, later on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wife and kids, God willing, and a business they could take on if they wanted. Same as my dad gave me.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, so nobody should **waste it**.
I'd tell **drifting friends** to start preparing now.
think: I'd be very **comfortable**, with time to build the business.
I could take over the **pharmacy** when my dad retires.
do: Keep the ward job a few years, then go **full time** on the business.
Learn the **pharmacy side** from my dad.
S4.quote: Give me ten years' warning and I'll be the one selling robot care visits, not the nurse losing his shifts to them.
fieldNote: A decade turns AI into **pure opportunity** for him.
He'd keep his **nursing registration**, linking the business to patient care.
His long-term picture is a **family business** passed down, like his father's.

steps.text: Move into the home respiratory business full time by 2030
Buy a second rental flat within three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years isn't long to build a business before robots arrive. If you're going to be replaced by a machine, you'd better be the one who owns the machine. What would help is less red tape for small health businesses and fair access to the new robots, not just for the big hospital chains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether nurses could own part of this. Everyone assumes nurses are employees forever, but some of us could run things, if the rules let us.

headlineQuote: If you're going to be replaced by a machine, you'd better be the one who owns the machine.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old** respiratory nurse at a **private hospital** who uses AI every day.
He's single, owns his flat plus a **rental studio**, and helps with his parents' pharmacy.
He plans a **home respiratory nursing** service and sees AI as cutting its costs.
He's **calm** in most worlds, and only **uneasy** in AGI by 2028, aiming to own the robots.
He favours **self-reliance** and family business over government support.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, leaving only **three years** to build a business before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Less red tape** for small health businesses.
**Fair access** to new robots, not just for big hospital chains.
